executive_summary: The analysis of four documents reveals a fundamental tension between official accounts of the Brumaire coup—the decree, proclamation, and constitution—and Bourrienne's memoir. While the official texts present the change of authority as a necessary act grounded in the failure of the prior constitution, Bourrienne's behind-the-scenes narrative emphasizes the coup's contingent nature and Napoleon Bonaparte's flawed public performance at St. Cloud. Together, these sources show that the same event can be portrayed as both a formal legal transfer and a high-risk personal enterprise.
key_findings: The official documents (the Brumaire decree and the Year VIII Constitution) establish the change of authority through formal legal mechanisms: the creation of a provisional consular commission (A0017) and the appointment of three consuls for ten years (A0002).
Bourrienne's memoir states that Bonaparte's remarks at St. Cloud were confused and devoid of dignity and sense (A0010, A0012), contradicting any later narratives claiming a coherent speech.
The memoir emphasizes the contingent nature of the coup, suggesting that failure and even Bonaparte's execution were real possibilities (A0009, A0013).
cross_cutting_patterns: Bourrienne's memoir characterizes Bonaparte's St. Cloud remarks as confused and undignified, while the official proclamation and decree present the coup as a necessary response to a failed constitution and corrupt Directory, creating a tension between the personal, contingent account and the official narrative of necessity.

actionable_recommendations.title: Expand the corpus to include additional contemporary memoirs and official speech texts
actionable_recommendations.description: To fully map the divergence between official and memoir accounts, extend this analysis to include full texts of revolutionary-era speeches (e.g., Bonaparte's alleged St. Cloud addresses) and other contemporary memoirs (e.g., Barras's or Sieyès's) that can corroborate or challenge Bourrienne's specific claim that no coherent speech was delivered.

actionable_recommendations.title: Increase textual coverage within existing document types
actionable_recommendations.description: Apply the same coding scheme to the full text of Bourrienne's memoir and the complete organic laws of the Year VIII Constitution to verify whether the observed pattern of legal formality versus contingent personal narrative holds consistently across larger samples.

actionable_recommendations.title: Investigate the dissemination and reception of official documents
actionable_recommendations.description: Analyze the specific audiences and publication contexts of the decree, proclamation, and constitution (e.g., were they posted publicly, read aloud, or archived?) to understand the intended reach and rhetorical effect of the official version of events, which this corpus alone does not reveal.

confidence_assessment.evidence: Direct, explicit textual evidence from the memoir that Bonaparte's speech was confused, incoherent, and stammered – supported by application references A0010 and A0012.

Multiple passages in the memoir (A0009, A0013) explicitly state that success was not inevitable and that failure could have led to Bonaparte's execution. This is robust internal evidence from a single source.

The official documents (A0017, A0002) clearly establish the legal framework of the new consular government. The contrast with Bourrienne's narrative is structurally clear, though the legal texts do not directly address the execution events.

analytical_memo: A key analytical decision was to treat Bourrienne's claim that no coherent speech was delivered at St. Cloud as a direct contradiction of any official narrative that later attributed formal speeches to Bonaparte—this was supported by explicit memoir text. A surprise was the degree to which Bourrienne's account of contingency (e.g., the risk of Bonaparte's execution) was supported by multiple passages and directly contrasted with the official documents' tone of crisis and necessity. Uncertainty remains about whether Bourrienne's memoir represents a corrective or a self-serving reinterpretation, and about the precise audience and reception of the official documents; these areas warrant further investigation with additional sources.
